format_adjustments.quarterback: devalued for 1QB and four-point passing touchdowns
format_adjustments.running_back_and_wide_receiver: elevated fit importance because the lineup starts three FLEX spots

draft_grade.haul: 2.06 Chris Bell, 3.04 Demond Claiborne, 3.12 Max Klare

editorial.headline: Solid values, modest ceiling
editorial.biggest_question: Whether Max Klare was the best use of a pick for the league's No. 2 TE room
editorial.summary: All three players beat or approximated expert consensus: Chris Bell ranked around 16 and went 18, Demond Claiborne ranked around 24 and went 28, and Max Klare ranked around 31 and went 36. The live market is cooler on the group than the experts, which adds real uncertainty.
editorial.fit_note: The roster is already deep and competitive, so it could afford value over need. Still, another tight end brings less marginal benefit in a no-premium format than an equivalent RB or WR swing would.
editorial.verdict: No obvious mistake and no obvious league-winner. This is a professional veteran-roster draft: take falling talent, preserve depth, and move on.

draft_grade.haul: 1.08 Denzel Boston, 3.08 Ty Simpson, 4.08 Brenen Thompson

editorial.headline: Drafting directly into the roster's empty spaces
editorial.biggest_question: Whether Denzel Boston was worth passing on the higher-ranked names at 1.08
editorial.summary: Denzel Boston was taken about two spots ahead of expert consensus, but the next two picks were sharp. Ty Simpson carried a consensus rank around 20 and lasted to 32; Brenen Thompson carried a rank around 37 and lasted to 44. Even in 1QB, Simpson is cheap enough at that price to justify the bet.
editorial.fit_note: This roster entered the draft first at RB but 11th at both QB and WR. All three picks attacked those weaknesses, which matters more in a lineup with three FLEX spots.
editorial.verdict: A small class with almost no wasted motion. Boston needs to hit for the grade to age into an A, but the Day 3 value and roster fit are excellent.

draft_grade.haul: 1.12 Ja'Kobi Lane, 2.09 Adam Randall, 3.03 Eli Raridon, 4.05 Colbie Young

editorial.headline: Four selections, four bets against the board
editorial.biggest_question: Why keep adding to the roster's strongest rooms
editorial.summary: Ja'Kobi Lane went at 1.12 with an expert median around 22, Adam Randall went at 2.09 with a median around 35, Eli Raridon went at 3.03 with a median around 32, and Colbie Young went at 4.05 with a median around 47. Every selection was ahead of consensus, and the first two were substantial reaches.
editorial.fit_note: The Ape already ranked second at WR and first at TE. In a no-TE-premium league, adding another tight end and two more receivers needed stronger value justification than the board supplied.
editorial.verdict: A contender can draft for conviction, but conviction is not free. Lane or Randall must become a clear outlier for this class to beat the opportunity cost.

draft_grade.haul: 1.01 Jeremiyah Love, 1.09 Jonah Coleman, 1.10 Kenyon Sadiq, 2.01 Omar Cooper, 2.10 Caleb Douglas, 3.01 Antonio Williams, 3.11 Malik Benson, 4.01 Bryce Lance, 4.09 Cade Klubnik

editorial.headline: Volume, volatility, and one enormous safety net
editorial.biggest_question: Why so much capital was spent ahead of consensus after the early wins
editorial.summary: Jeremiyah Love at 1.01 was automatic, Kenyon Sadiq at 1.10 was fair value, and Omar Cooper at 2.01 was a major consensus win. Antonio Williams at 3.01 and Bryce Lance at 4.01 were also discounted. But Jonah Coleman went a few spots early, Caleb Douglas went roughly a round early by expert consensus, and Malik Benson was another aggressive bet.
editorial.fit_note: The repeated WR swings correctly attack a bottom-three room, and the roster can absorb developmental players because the league provides 14 bench and two taxi spots.
editorial.verdict: Eight picks produced several genuine wins and several avoidable reaches. Love creates a high floor for the class; the middle-round efficiency keeps it from earning an A.

draft_grade.haul: 1.02 Jordyn Tyson, 1.05 KC Concepcion, 1.11 Fernando Mendoza, 2.03 Cyrus Allen, 2.05 Emmett Johnson, 3.02 Eli Stowers, 3.07 Kaelon Black

editorial.headline: A huge class that never fully chose between value and conviction
editorial.summary: Jordyn Tyson, KC Concepcion, and Fernando Mendoza were all slightly early but defensible. The class swung sharply at 2.03, where Cyrus Allen went about two rounds ahead of the expert median, though the live market is considerably more optimistic. The recovery was strong: Emmett Johnson was reasonable, Eli Stowers was a major value, and Kaelon Black beat consensus.
editorial.fit_note: The two RB selections correctly attack the league's 12th-ranked RB room. Mendoza is less valuable here than on generic boards because this is 1QB with four-point passing touchdowns.
editorial.verdict: There is enough talent and volume for this class to work, but Stowers and Black are doing too much repair work after the Allen reach. The model is more forgiving because live traders like Allen; the editorial grade prices in the opportunity cost.

draft_grade.haul: 1.03 Carnell Tate, 3.05 Kaytron Allen, 4.03 Seth McGowan

editorial.headline: A rebuild with an actual thesis
editorial.biggest_question: Whether either late RB dart becomes more than depth
editorial.summary: Final Boss took the consensus rookie No. 2 at 1.03, then used discounted picks on the roster's weakest room. Kaytron Allen was essentially market value at 3.05; Seth McGowan was a mild reach, but a fourth-round reach at a position of need is the right kind of miss to risk.
editorial.fit_note: The league's No. 12 roster needed a foundational asset more than immediate points. Tate supplies that, while two RB swings attack an RB room ranked 11th.
editorial.verdict: The cleanest marriage of value and team direction in the league. The haul does not finish the rebuild, but it gives the rebuild a face.

editorial.headline: Correct position, average prices
editorial.biggest_question: Whether two mid-tier receivers materially fix the league's weakest WR room
editorial.summary: Germie Bernard was taken four spots ahead of expert consensus, while Zachariah Branch lasted a couple of spots beyond it. The two picks roughly cancel out on pure value.
editorial.fit_note: No team needed receivers more: Gridiron Geezers entered the draft 12th at WR, and three FLEX spots make that weakness especially expensive.
editorial.verdict: The board value is ordinary, but the roster logic is impeccable. Branch is the pick with the better chance to make this class look clever.

editorial.headline: Need-driven and mostly sensible
editorial.biggest_question: Whether Matt Hibner's athletic bet can overcome the opportunity cost
editorial.summary: Nicholas Singleton was almost exactly consensus value at 2.04 and addressed a weak RB room. Matt Hibner was selected well ahead of the expert median, though the live market was somewhat less skeptical.
editorial.fit_note: RB and TE ranked 10th and 12th before the draft, so both selections attacked real needs. The no-TE-premium setting means Hibner needs to become a legitimate starter—not merely an interesting athlete—to return value.
editorial.verdict: Singleton is the type of boring-correct pick that keeps a draft afloat. Hibner determines whether this finishes as a B or slides toward a C.

editorial.headline: One value pick, one luxury reach
editorial.biggest_question: Why add Drew Allar to the league's No. 3 QB room in a 1QB format
editorial.summary: Skyler Bell was a consensus top-27 rookie who fell to 33, a clean value. Drew Allar was closer to 42nd by expert consensus and went 34th. The live market likes Allar more than the rankers do, but the league settings and roster context both reduce the payoff.
editorial.fit_note: The roster's weakest room was TE, not QB. In superflex the Allar bet would be defensible; with one quarterback and four-point passing touchdowns, it is a luxury selection.
editorial.verdict: Bell saves the class from a lower grade. Allar now needs either a meaningful value spike or a trade market to justify the opportunity cost.

draft_grade.haul: 1.07 De'Zhaun Stribling, 2.07 Malachi Fields, 2.08 Elijah Sarratt, 4.02 Eli Heidenreich, 4.07 Justin Joly

editorial.headline: A good roster drafted like it could afford to be picky
editorial.biggest_question: The cumulative opportunity cost of taking three receivers ahead of consensus
editorial.summary: De'Zhaun Stribling at 1.07 was the largest early bet, with an expert median around 13. Malachi Fields and Elijah Sarratt were smaller reaches. The late picks were better: Eli Heidenreich was close to value and Justin Joly was discounted.
editorial.fit_note: Receiver was the roster's weakest starting room, so the positional plan was sensible. The problem was price, not purpose.
editorial.verdict: This draft may look better in a year if one of the three receivers separates from the tier. Today it reads as repeated conviction without enough board discipline.

draft_grade.haul: 1.04 Jadarian Price, 1.06 Makai Lemon, 2.12 Mike Washington, 3.06 Ted Hurst, 4.06 Oscar Delp

editorial.headline: Five bets, three steals, one coherent retool
editorial.biggest_question: Whether Mike Washington's market enthusiasm outruns his blocked depth chart
editorial.summary: Jadarian Price was a defensible need pick one slot ahead of expert consensus. Makai Lemon was the opposite: a consensus top-four rookie acquired at 1.06. The draft then turned into a value hunt—Hurst was ranked 19th by the expert median and went 30th, while Oscar Delp was ranked 30th and went 42nd. Mike Washington is the swing pick: experts place him around 26th, but the live trade market already values him around 15th.
editorial.fit_note: Price and Washington directly attack a pre-draft RB room ranked 10th; Lemon and Hurst add needed WR succession; Delp fits the open rookie-taxi runway without forcing TE-premium economics onto the grade.
editorial.verdict: This is how a lower-tier roster should use five selections: add two players who can enter the lineup, then layer in asymmetric upside. It does not make Terry Tate's Pain Train a contender by itself, but it creates multiple paths to becoming one.

editorial.headline: The league favorite is finally on the clock
editorial.biggest_question: Whether the final pick can address a TE room ranked 10th or simply preserve value
editorial.summary: Bronco Stampede has not selected through 4.08 and is on the clock at 4.09. A single late pick cannot materially change the league's No. 1 roster, but it can still produce a useful taxi or trade asset.
editorial.fit_note: This is the strongest roster in the league, with elite QB and WR rooms. Tight end is the only relative weakness, though value should still beat need this late.
editorial.verdict: No grade until the selection is made. The larger story is that the favorite entered the rookie draft without needing it to rescue anything.
